node.label: Penny Summerfield
node.date_label: Women Workers (1984; 1989 republication) · Reconstructing Women’s Wartime Lives (1998) · Culture and Composure (2004) · Histories of the Self (2018 release; 2019 imprint)
node.description: In Reconstructing Women’s Wartime Lives (1998), Penny Summerfield examines how public representations of wartime men and women shape women’s retrospective accounts of their own lives. The composure approach developed in “Culture and Composure” (2004) asks how telling a life story can produce psychic ease, and how available cultural narratives can obstruct that process. Earlier research on women’s wartime employment distinguished changes in occupation and work arrangements from the removal of gender hierarchy. “Oral History as an Autobiographical Practice” (2016) argues that oral history has become an autobiographical practice in which understanding how subjectivity is constituted in an interview is more urgent; Histories of the Self (released in 2018, with a 2019 imprint) extends methodological discussion across personal narrative genres. Jon Lawrence explicitly credits Summerfield’s work on intersubjectivity in his 2022 account of reusing social-science archives. Lucy Newby and Fearghus Roulston (2026) value the analytical space opened by Summerfield’s composure model but caution that fragmented narration can be creative expression rather than evidence of an inability to tell a coherent story. Summerfield’s 2023 study of wartime correspondence applies composure to letter writing, using Foucault’s technologies of the self to investigate gendered anxiety and family separation.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Women Workers in the Second World War (1984); Out of the Cage: Women’s Experiences in Two World Wars, with Gail Braybon (1987); Reconstructing Women’s Wartime Lives (1998); “Dis/composing the Subject,” in Feminism and Autobiography (2000); “Culture and Composure” (2004); “Oral History as an Autobiographical Practice” (2016); Histories of the Self: Personal Narratives and Historical Practice (2018); “My Heart Is a Piece of Stone” (2023).
node.scope_note: Full monographs, the 2000 chapter and original 2004 article remain unread. The 1998 book is known through publisher description and the author’s historiographical essay; the 2004 framework through the author’s selected 2023 passages and Newby/Roulston’s 2026 discussion. Only the 2016 abstract and indexed excerpts were accessible. The 2018 departmental essay was read in full; selected 2023 and 2026 passages, not complete articles, were read. Cited Foucault and Bourke originals and the underlying archival letters were not independently read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “On Historians’ Re-Use of Social-Science Archives” (2022), Lawrence explicitly acknowledges a debt to Summerfield’s “Dis/composing the Subject” (2000) for his treatment of intersubjectivity in “Social-Science Encounters” (2014).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lawrence, p. 439, paragraph beginning “My 2014 article” and n. 25: “My debt has been principally to oral historians,” immediately naming Summerfield’s chapter. Publisher HTML argument and note read. The 2000 chapter and complete 2014 article remain unread; no claim that all of Lawrence’s method derives from Summerfield.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “‘My Heart Is a Piece of Stone’” (2023), Summerfield applies Foucault’s “technologies of the self” (1988) to letter writing as a practice of managing identities and emotions during wartime separation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: “Epistolarity, Love, and Marriage,” opening paragraph, callout n. 16; conclusion, opening two paragraphs. Summerfield explicitly names the concept and n. 16 identifies Foucault’s 1988 seminar text as its origin. Selected primary passages read; the Foucault text is unread here. This establishes a specific conceptual resource, without a general allegiance claim.
proposed_edges.map_label: Letters as technologies of the self

proposed_edges.relationship: Reconstructing Women’s Wartime Lives (1998) investigates how public representations of wartime men and women interact with women’s retrospective accounts of their own lives.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: MUP publisher description and August 1998 metadata read; the monograph remains unread. Claim confined to the stated research question, corroborated by the author’s 1998 essay, pp. 222–224.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Research on women in Britain in the Second World War” (1998), Summerfield interprets wartime employment change through occupational redistribution and gender segregation rather than a simple expulsion of women from paid work after the war.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Section I, pp. 210–213: author’s synthesis of earlier findings, including the 1984 Women Workers book (1989 republication). Those originals unread. No general claim about all belligerent countries.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Research on women in Britain in the Second World War” (1998), Summerfield treats wartime welfare as compromises between production needs and patriarchal expectations that left women reconciling paid work and domestic responsibilities.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Section II, pp. 214–215, especially the paragraphs distinguishing her analysis from Riley’s. This is the author’s 1998 retrospective synthesis; the earlier 1983 article and book remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In "Oral History as an Autobiographical Practice" (2016), Summerfield argues that oral history has become an autobiographical practice centred on the narrator's subjectivity, making it more urgent to understand how subjectivity is constituted in an interview, a shift she says challenges how history itself is conceptualized.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete author abstract in the Manchester repository read. Full journal article not accessible; no detailed interview analysis attributed on this basis. The abstract preserves recovery history’s continuing value alongside the autobiographical approach.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Histories of the Self” (2018), Summerfield explains how historians interpret evasions, silences and interactions between spoken memory and popular culture when using personal testimony.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author’s departmental essay, paragraph beginning “It reviews historians’ attempts,” with the preceding discussion of referentiality and subjectivity. Essay read in full; this claim concerns the 2018 methodological self-account, not an independently read monograph.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “‘My Heart Is a Piece of Stone’” (2023), Summerfield uses wartime correspondence to study gendered anxiety, maternal subjectivity and family separation, extending composure analysis from interviews to letter writing.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Abstract; introduction’s final paragraph; conclusion, first four paragraphs and n. 146. These selected primary passages explicitly connect fluent writing and psychic ease, and analyze their breakdown. The case is not presented as statistically representative; complete middle case study and archival letters unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Oral History as an Autobiographical Practice” (2016), Summerfield argues that recovery projects such as Thompson’s large-scale study of Edwardian working lives, which strove for representativeness, faced major difficulties of sample and questionnaire, since no statistically representative sample of a past population can be obtained and interviews are dialogic.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read on OpenEdition (Miranda 12, 2016, online 1 April 2016), section on recovery history. ¶7 names “oral historians such as Paul Thompson, who undertook a large-scale project on Edwardian working lives” (with Elizabeth Roberts on Lancashire women), says they “strove for representativeness”, then: “However well-intentioned, such endeavours faced major difficulties, relating to the sample and the questionnaire” and “It is not possible to obtain a statistically representative sample of any population in the past”; a standard questionnaire does not suit a dialogic interview. Bibliography: Thompson, The Edwardians (1975); The Voice of the Past (1978). ¶¶5–6 also report, without dispute, Thompson’s account of oral history’s origins and his defence of memory’s reliability (Thompson 1978). A qualified methodological critique of the recovery programme’s sampling aim, not a rejection of Thompson’s work. The Edwardians unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions representative sampling in oral history

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Oral History as an Autobiographical Practice” (2016), Summerfield uses Scott’s “The Evidence of Experience” (1991), the point that accounts of experience cannot give direct access to social reality, to frame her critique of recovery history and her case that subjectivity is constructed in the interview.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read on OpenEdition (Miranda 12, 2016). ¶10: the telling of experience is, “according to post-structural theorists Joan W Scott and Judith Butler, the means by which subjects constitute themselves”, followed by “Subjectivity is constructed through the language of the interchange in an oral history interview” (Scott 1991; Butler 1990). ¶11, on critiques of recovery history: “as Joan W. Scott has pointed out, accounts of experience cannot give direct access to social reality” (Scott 1991). Bibliography: Scott, “The Evidence of Experience,” Critical Inquiry 17.4 (1991): 773–797. Body-text use of Scott’s argument at two points, the second attributed to Scott alone. Butler is named only jointly with Scott and is not proposed. Limits: a named conceptual resource in a methodological essay, not a claim that Scott shaped Summerfield’s earlier work; the 1998 monograph and 2004 article remain unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Scott’s ‘evidence of experience’ in oral history

proposed_edges.relationship: In Histories of the Self: Personal Narratives and Historical Practice (2018; 2019 imprint), Summerfield contributes to historical life writing by examining how historians interpret autobiographies and memoirs, particularly their selectivity and the influence of the present on accounts of the past.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Evans's complete review on the journal publisher's site. Its chapter-four discussion identifies genre, selective recollection and the narrator's present as methodological problems in autobiography. This supports a scoped contribution to life-writing methods. Summerfield's book was not read in full; no claim of founding the field or of influence on a particular eligible historian is made.

proposed_edges.relationship: In New Directions in Social and Cultural History (2018), the editors cite Summerfield's chapter 'Subjectivity, the self and historical practice' as the volume's discussion of new cultural history's turn towards histories of selfhood and subjectivity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the introduction in the licensed publisher preview. The passage explicitly names Summerfield's chapter while explaining a methodological development within new cultural history. The preview establishes the chapter title and 2018 publication year. The chapter itself falls outside the preview and remains unread. The edge records this identified intervention, without inferring personal intellectual transmission to the editors.
